summary: RoadmapBench: 115 long-horizon tasks built from real consecutive release pairs of 17 open-source repos in Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust and C++. The agent starts at the source version and gets a multi-target 'roadmap' instruction (median 5 targets; oracle median ~3,714 lines across 51 files) and is scored per target by adapted upstream tests. Thirteen frontier models under OpenHands resolve 5.2%–39.1% of tasks.

claims.claim: Even the strongest model (Claude-Opus-4.7) resolves only 39.1%; the weakest 5.2%.
claims.evidence: Table 2 / §4.2 under OpenHands, 115 tasks — numbers match abstract. Single trial per model (Table 2 caption), no CIs on headline numbers.

claims.claim: Long-horizon multi-target development is much harder than bug-fix benchmarks.
claims.evidence: Contrast to '80%+ on SWE-bench Verified' is cited, not measured on the same harness; difficulty declines monotonically with files/lines/targets (Fig. 7, Wilson CIs).

claims.claim: Top models are scaffold-robust; mid/low-tier models swing 3–10 pp between OpenHands and Terminus 2.
claims.evidence: §5.4: Claude-Opus-4.6 31.3% vs 32.2%; DeepSeek-V4-Pro +7.9 pp on OpenHands; GLM-5.1 and Qwen3.6-Plus better on Terminus 2. Single trial each, subset of models, so 1–3 pp differences are within noise.

claims.claim: Strong models fail mostly on implementation correctness; weak models on build errors/missing code.
claims.evidence: §5.6 over 3,603 failed subtasks, classified by Claude-Sonnet-4.6; classifier validated at 88% category agreement with experts (App. H.1).

claims.claim: Task quality is assured by static validation and rollout-based QC.
claims.evidence: App. G.3: 45/115 tasks needed fixes (avg 3.1 rounds); Cohen's κ=0.83 on 40 trajectories; QC raised Claude-Opus-4.6 resolved rate 19.1%→30.4% (Table 4), showing ~1/3 of initial failures were task defects.

patterns.note: New version-upgrade, multi-target benchmark with partial-credit Completion Score.
Roadmap instructions specify API signatures, defaults, exception behavior per target; partial-credit scoring per target shows agents complete several targets then stall at integration.
Execution-based grading; strong models' trajectories spend more on edit+execute than exploration (§5.2), suggestive not causal.
Single-agent OpenHands/Terminus 2 loops only; no multi-agent or planner harness tested.

[retag 2026-10-08] Agents have no clarification channel; task defects are repaired by the benchmark builders instead. Rollout QC (App. G.3, Table 4) found task-side defects in 45/115 tasks (instruction gaps, brittle tests, environment and grading errors; average 3.1 fix rounds). Repairing them raised Claude-Opus-4.6 from 19.1% to 30.4% resolved, GLM-5.1 +3.0 and Kimi-K2.5 +1.0. This shows the cost of unstated requirements, not whether an agent asking about them helps.

methodology.baselines: Models compared to each other; two scaffolds (OpenHands for all, Terminus 2 for a subset). No harness variants (planning, sub-agents, test-first) tested.
methodology.models: Claude-Opus-4.7/4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6/K2.5, Mimo-V2.5-Pro, Qwen3.6-Plus, Qwen3.5-397B, MiniMax-M2.7, Seed-2.0-Pro; reasoning effort differs per model (xhigh for Opus-4.7, high for some, default for others).
methodology.variance: Single trial per model; Wilson CIs only on complexity bins.
methodology.ablations: Scaffold sensitivity, step budget, complexity proxies, QC before/after.
methodology.contamination_controls: Future branches/tags pruned, repo names and versions anonymized in instructions; but target-version code of popular repos (Polars, Prisma, Ruff...) is public and may be in pretraining data — not measured.
methodology.languages: Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust, C++; no Java.

standards.artifacts: Tasks packaged as Harbor environments; no repository/dataset URL found in the text.

biases.detail: Single trial per model; scaffold differences of 1–3 pp are interpreted as patterns.
Target versions of popular public repos predate model cutoffs; anonymization of instructions does not prevent memorized code.
QC keeps tasks only if models of different tiers produce distinguishable scores and repairs task defects found via model rollouts — benchmark is shaped by the models it ranks.
Uneven reasoning-effort settings across models (xhigh vs high vs default) confound the model ranking.
No dataset URL in the paper text.

coi.affiliations: UniPat AI, Peking University, Fudan University, University of Hong Kong, Tsinghua University, 0G Labs, Pipeline Lab (per-author mapping not recoverable from extracted text).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Thirteen third-party frontier models; no author affiliation with a ranked model vendor identified.
coi.detail: Some company affiliations (UniPat AI, 0G Labs, Pipeline Lab), but they do not appear to ship a ranked model or the scaffolds tested.

verdict_reason: Well-built benchmark with real multi-target version-upgrade tasks, partial-credit scoring, QC with inter-annotator agreement, and a validated failure classifier; headline numbers are in the body. Caveats: single trials, uneven reasoning-effort settings, no Java, no released artifact URL, and QC that tunes tasks against the evaluated models.
applicability: Useful calibration for the Java team: multi-target feature work spanning ~50 files is where agents fail (≤39% fully resolved) and they typically finish some targets then break at integration/wiring — exactly the shape of cross-repo cross-repository changes. Implication: in spec-driven development, split specs into separately testable targets with per-target acceptance tests (the paper's per-target scoring is a template), and gate integration explicitly. Results do not include Java and use single-repo tasks, so they likely overstate what agents can do across ≥4 coordinated repos. Scaffold-robustness of top models suggests mixed agent hosts matter less than model tier for frontier models, but this rests on single runs.

conflicts_with.detail: RoadmapBench reports top models are scaffold-robust (<1 pp between OpenHands and Terminus 2); the 'Scaffold Effect' paper's title asserts harness choice is a hidden variable. Not verified against that paper's body — check magnitude/model tiers before treating as a contradiction.
